schema.description: The Moog Minimoog (Model D) is a monophonic analog synthesizer introduced in 1970, one of the most influential synthesizers ever made.

sections.whatItIs: The Moog Minimoog — properly the Model D — is the monophonic analog synthesizer that defined what a synth could be. Introduced in 1970, it put three oscillators and Moog's celebrated 24 dB ladder filter into a single portable, performance-ready instrument, and its fat, vocal lead and bass tones run through five decades of records. Original units were built into the early 1980s; Moog Music reissued the Model D in 2016 and in later runs, so the name now spans both vintage and current production.
sections.buyingUsed: The first question is era: an early-1970s original, a late Norlin-era unit, and a modern reissue are three different instruments at three different price points, and listings don't always make the distinction clear. Vintage units are prized but high-maintenance — expect oscillator tuning drift, scratchy potentiometers, worn keyboard bushings and contacts, and tired pitch and mod wheels; many benefit from a proper calibration and service. Later originals and the reissues are considerably more stable, and the reissue adds modern conveniences like MIDI and a CV patchbay. For any vintage unit, ask about recent servicing and how well it holds tuning once warm — that's the real tell.
sections.regionalNotes: Vintage Minimoogs surface less often in Japan than Roland's home-grown gear, but they do appear on Yahoo Auctions and Mercari, and the reissues circulate domestically through the usual shops. Watch voltage in both directions: a US vintage unit is 117V, a Japanese-market unit is 100V, and neither runs happily on European mains without a transformer. In Japanese listings the instrument is written モーグ or, in older transliteration, ムーグ (Moog), alongside ミニモーグ (Minimoog) and モデルD (Model D); the same condition vocabulary applies — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent condition), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested). Because the transliteration itself varies, a search that only looks for "Minimoog" in Latin script misses part of the market — one of the gaps Brrtz is designed to catch.

schema.description: The ARP 2600 is a semi-modular analog synthesizer introduced in 1971, prized for its patchable architecture and distinctive sound.

sections.whatItIs: The ARP 2600 is a semi-modular analog synthesizer introduced in 1971 — a self-contained patchable system with three oscillators, a slider for every parameter, a bank of patch points, and on most units a built-in spring reverb and speakers. Played without a single patch cable it's already a complete synth; patched, it opens into a small modular studio. It's one of the most recorded synthesizers in history, and Korg's reissues brought it back into current production.
sections.buyingUsed: With the 2600, the single most important detail is the filter. The earliest units used a 4012 filter — a close cousin of Moog's ladder design, which is what triggered the famous lawsuit — and ARP later switched to the 4072; the early 4012 units sound distinct and command a premium, so confirm which one a vintage listing actually has. Beyond that, the collector hierarchy runs from the earliest "Blue Marvin" and "Grey Meanie" cases through the more common later black-and-orange units. On any vintage unit, check the sliders (they get noisy and need cleaning), the patch jacks, and the internal speaker and reverb tank — and remember the keyboard (the 3620) was a separate piece, so a "2600" without a keyboard is common and priced accordingly. Korg's reissues (the full-size 2600 FS and the smaller 2600 M) are the stable, affordable way in, and shouldn't be confused with a vintage unit in a listing title.
sections.regionalNotes: Korg is a Japanese company, so the reissues are well-distributed across the domestic market and turn up regularly on Yahoo Auctions, Mercari, and through Japanese shops — often the cleanest route to a 2600 FS or 2600 M. Genuine vintage 2600s appear too, though less frequently and at collector prices. Voltage still applies: domestic units are 100V and need a transformer abroad. In Japanese listings, look for アープ (ARP) and 2600, or コルグ (Korg) for the reissues, and read the condition terms — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested). Brrtz surfaces these across both the Japanese and Western source groups in a single scan.

schema.description: The Roland TR-808 Rhythm Composer is a programmable analog drum machine produced from 1980 to 1983, foundational to hip-hop, techno, and pop production.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland TR-808 Rhythm Composer is a programmable analog drum machine built in Japan between 1980 and 1983. Its sounds are entirely synthesized rather than sampled — the booming, tunable kick, the metallic cowbell, the snappy clap, the sizzling hats — and that synthetic character, once dismissed as unrealistic, became the backbone of hip-hop, electro, techno, and modern pop. Roland made only around twelve thousand units before discontinuing it, which is a large part of why clean originals now command the prices they do.
sections.buyingUsed: First, confirm you're looking at an original and not a descendant. Roland's own TR-08 (Boutique) and TR-8S model the 808 digitally, and Behringer's RD-8 is an analog clone — all capable machines, none of them an original 808, and listing titles routinely blur the line. On a genuine unit, the usual age-related issues are aging electrolytic capacitors, drifting or dead voice cards, scratchy pots and switches, and tired trigger contacts; a recent recap or service is a meaningful plus. Remember the 808 predates MIDI — it speaks DIN sync only, so budget for a sync converter or an installed MIDI retrofit if you need to lock it to a DAW.
sections.regionalNotes: Because the 808 was manufactured in Japan, the domestic used market is unusually deep. Yahoo Auctions (ヤフオク) and Mercari regularly surface units that never left the country, often in cleaner cosmetic condition and below Western dealer pricing. The catch is voltage: domestic Japanese units are 100V and need a step-up transformer to run safely on 117V or 230V mains. In Japanese listings the gear appears under ローランド (Roland), リズムコンポーザー (Rhythm Composer), and simply 808 — and the condition vocabulary is where the real risk and value sit. 動作確認済み (tested working) and 整備済み (serviced) are reassuring; 美品 means excellent cosmetic condition; while ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested) mean sold as-is and should be priced accordingly. This cross-border gap is exactly what Brrtz is built to close.

schema.description: The Roland Juno-106 is a 6-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer released in 1984, known for its DCO oscillators, warm chorus, and MIDI.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland Juno-106, released in 1984, is the polyphonic analog synth that taught a generation what "warm" means. Six voices, one digitally controlled oscillator each, a genuine analog low-pass filter, and Roland's lush stereo chorus give it a sound that's instantly recognizable across house, synth-pop, and ambient records. Its layout is famously immediate — a slider or switch for nearly everything — and full MIDI made it the first classic polysynth many producers could actually integrate into a modern setup.
sections.buyingUsed: The Juno-106's signature weakness is its voice chips — the 80017A modules that carry each voice. Their internal resin degrades and shorts over time, producing dropouts, stuck notes, or dead voices; it's the single most important thing to test, so ask the seller to confirm all six voices play cleanly across the keyboard. Reproduction 80017A chips are widely available and a common repair, so a unit with one or two bad voices isn't a dealbreaker if it's priced for it. Beyond the voice chips, check the sliders and the membrane-style buttons, and listen for a healthy chorus — a noisy or silent chorus is another known age issue.
sections.regionalNotes: As a Roland product the Juno-106 is abundant in Japan and among the cleanest-value routes to one; Yahoo Auctions and Mercari list them regularly, often below Western dealer prices. Voltage is the usual catch — domestic units are 100V and want a step-up transformer abroad. In Japanese listings look for ローランド (Roland) and ジュノ or ジュノー (Juno), and read condition terms carefully — 動作確認済み (tested working) and 整備済み (serviced) are reassuring, 美品 means excellent cosmetic condition, and ジャンク (junk) or 未確認 (untested) mean as-is, which for a 106 often signals unaddressed voice-chip problems. Brrtz scans the Japanese and Western sources together so you can compare a serviced domestic unit against local listings in one pass.

schema.description: The Roland TB-303 Bass Line is a monophonic analog synthesizer and sequencer released in 1981 that became the defining sound of acid house.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland TB-303 Bass Line, released in 1981, was a commercial flop as the bass-guitar substitute it was marketed to be — and then became one of the most influential instruments ever made. Its squelchy, resonant filter sweep and quirky built-in sequencer created the sound of acid house, and originals now trade at prices wildly disconnected from their humble origins. It's a single-oscillator mono synth with a sawtooth and a square wave, but the magic is in the accent, slide, and filter behavior that no spec sheet captures.
sections.buyingUsed: Because genuine 303s are expensive and small, authenticity and condition are everything — and clones are everywhere. Roland's own TB-03 (Boutique) and the TD-3 from Behringer recreate the sound convincingly but are not originals, and listing titles blur this constantly, so confirm you're looking at a real 1980s TB-303. On a genuine unit, check the battery compartment for corrosion (leaked batteries are a common source of damage), test every function of the sequencer, and confirm the filter sweeps smoothly. Given the values involved, insist on clear photos of the serial and internals, and treat any as-is original with appropriate caution.
sections.regionalNotes: The 303 is Japanese-built and appears on Yahoo Auctions and Mercari, though rarely and at collector prices — the domestic market is no longer the bargain it once was for this particular box, but clean units and honest condition descriptions still surface. Voltage applies as ever: domestic units are 100V. In Japanese listings look for ローランド (Roland) and simply 303, and weigh the condition vocabulary heavily — 動作確認済み (tested working) and 整備済み (serviced) matter a great deal on an instrument this valuable, while ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested) demand real scrutiny. Brrtz surfaces 303 listings across Japanese and Western sources at once so you can gauge the true market rather than a single region's.

schema.description: The Roland SH-101 is a monophonic analog synthesizer released in 1982, popular for its portability, bright sound, and built-in sequencer.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland SH-101, released in 1982, is a monophonic analog synth that punches far above its modest size. A single oscillator with sub-oscillator, a punchy filter, an onboard sequencer and arpeggiator, and an optional modulation grip that let it be worn like a keytar made it a favorite for basslines, leads, and acid — and its bright, direct sound keeps it in constant demand. Roland sold it in grey, red, and blue, and the colored versions carry a small premium among collectors.
sections.buyingUsed: The SH-101 is relatively robust, but age still shows up in the usual analog places: scratchy sliders and pots, worn keyboard contacts, and occasionally a flaky sequencer or battery-related memory issues. Test the sequencer and arpeggiator thoroughly, confirm the sub-oscillator and filter respond smoothly, and check the pitch bender. Behringer's MS-1 is a well-regarded modern clone with the same core voice, so make sure a listing is actually an original SH-101 and not a clone. The detachable mod grip and matching strap are frequently missing — nice to have, but not essential to the instrument.
sections.regionalNotes: As a Roland classic the SH-101 is plentiful in Japan and often keenly priced on Yahoo Auctions and Mercari, including the sought-after red and blue variants. schema.description: The Roland Jupiter-8 is an 8-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer introduced in 1981, one of Roland's flagship vintage instruments.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland Jupiter-8, introduced in 1981, is Roland's flagship vintage polysynth and one of the most coveted analog instruments ever built. Eight voices, two oscillators each, a flexible dual-filter design, and a famously lush, wide sound made it a staple of 1980s records, and clean originals now command serious money. It's big, heavy, and gorgeous — a centerpiece instrument rather than a utility box — and later units added the DCB interface that MIDI kits can build on.
sections.buyingUsed: At Jupiter-8 prices, condition and completeness dominate the decision. Vintage units need periodic service: expect potential issues with the many sliders and switches, aging power supplies, voice-board calibration, and the membrane-style panel. Ask about recent servicing, whether all eight voices are calibrated and stable, and whether any MIDI retrofit (the original has no MIDI) has been professionally installed. Roland's modern Jupiter-8 emulations — plug-outs and reissue-style hardware — are excellent but are not the vintage instrument, so read listing titles carefully. Given the values, insist on thorough photos and a clear account of any repairs.
sections.regionalNotes: The Jupiter-8 is Japanese-built, and while never common, it does appear on Yahoo Auctions and through Japanese dealers, sometimes in cleaner condition than Western examples — though rarely at bargain prices anymore. Domestic units are 100V and require a transformer abroad, a real consideration on an instrument this valuable. In Japanese listings look for ローランド (Roland), ジュピター (Jupiter), and JP-8, and weigh condition terms heavily — 動作確認済み (tested working) and 整備済み (serviced) are important, while ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested) warrant caution. schema.description: The Sequential Prophet-5 is a 5-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer first released in 1978, the first fully programmable polyphonic synth.

sections.whatItIs: The Prophet-5, first released by Sequential Circuits in 1978, was the world's first fully programmable polyphonic synthesizer — you could store and recall patches, which changed how synths were played and built. Five voices, two oscillators each, and Sequential's rich, immediate sound made it a defining instrument of its era, heard across countless records. Vintage units come in revisions (Rev 1 and 2 with SSM chips, Rev 3 with CEM chips) that sound subtly different, and Sequential's 2020 reissue brought the design back under founder Dave Smith.
sections.buyingUsed: Revision matters both sonically and practically. The earliest Rev 1 and Rev 2 units use SSM chips and are prized for their tone but are the most temperamental — tuning stability and chip availability are real concerns; Rev 3 units are more stable and more common. Whichever you consider, ask about tuning stability once warm, recent calibration or service, and the state of the potentiometers and switches. Be clear about vintage versus the modern reissue (the 2020 Prophet-5/Prophet-10), which is a superb instrument but not a vintage piece — titles often just say Prophet-5. At these prices, documentation of servicing is worth a lot.
sections.regionalNotes: The Prophet-5 is American-built, so vintage units surface less often in Japan than home-grown Roland or Korg gear — but they do appear on Yahoo Auctions and through Japanese dealers, and the reissue circulates domestically. Voltage runs both ways: a US vintage unit is 117V and a Japanese-market unit is 100V, so confirm which you're buying. In Japanese listings look for シーケンシャル (Sequential) and プロフェット (Prophet); the standard condition vocabulary applies — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested). schema.description: The Yamaha DX7 is a digital FM synthesizer released in 1983, one of the best-selling synthesizers of all time.

sections.whatItIs: The Yamaha DX7, released in 1983, is the digital FM synthesizer that defined the sound of the mid-1980s and became one of the best-selling synths ever made. Its six-operator FM engine produced the glassy electric pianos, bright basses, and bell tones that saturate the era's records, and it was among the first affordable fully digital, fully MIDI synths — which is a big part of why it sold in the hundreds of thousands. Programming it from the front panel is famously unintuitive, but its factory and cartridge sounds alone earned it a permanent place in studios.
sections.buyingUsed: The DX7 is digital, so it sidesteps analog tuning drift, but it has its own age issues. The original DX7's battery backs up patch memory and eventually dies — a cheap fix, but a dead battery plus lost patches is common; the membrane buttons can get unresponsive; and the notoriously fragile early data cartridges and their contacts often fail. Test the buttons, the output for noise, and ideally patch storage. Note the family: the original DX7, the DX7II (DX7S and DX7IID), and later variants differ, and the small FB-01, the TX-series, and the reface DX share the engine but aren't the same instrument — read titles carefully.
sections.regionalNotes: The DX7 is Yamaha, Japanese-built and sold in huge numbers, so Japan's used market is deep and often cheap — Yahoo Auctions, Mercari, and Hard Off regularly list them, frequently below Western prices. Domestic units are 100V and need a transformer abroad. In Japanese listings search ヤマハ (Yamaha) and DX7, and read condition terms — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested); on a DX7 junk often just means a dead memory battery, which can make for a bargain if you're willing to service it. Original units use one of two filter revisions that sound subtly different, worth noting if tone is your priority. On any vintage unit, check the patch jacks, the sliders and switches, the keyboard contacts, and confirm both filters self-oscillate cleanly; the original's non-standard mini-jack patch points are also worth verifying. Ask about servicing on older units.

sections.whatItIs: The Akai MPC3000, released in 1994, is the sampler-sequencer that anchored a golden era of hip-hop production. Designed by Roger Linn, it paired 16-bit sampling with a swing-savvy sequencer and those famous velocity-sensitive pads, and its workflow — chop, lay out on the pads, sequence, and let the timing feel do the rest — shaped the sound of countless records. It's a workstation, not a synth: no oscillators, just your samples, its sequencer, and its particular groove.
sections.buyingUsed: The MPC3000 is a 1990s computer at heart, so age shows in its subsystems. The backlit LCD often fails or dims and is a known replacement item; the floppy drive is a common weak point (many owners fit modern floppy-emulator drives); the battery that backs up memory dies; and the pad sensors can get uneven and need re-sensing or replacement. Test every pad for even response, the screen, and data storage. Note the variants and the surrounding family — the MPC60 before it and the MPC2000 and 2000XL after — plus the Vailixi OS mod that many units run; a listing should be clear about what it is and what's been serviced or upgraded.
sections.regionalNotes: Akai is Japanese, and MPCs are plentiful in Japan's used market — Yahoo Auctions, Mercari, and Hard Off list the 3000 and its siblings regularly, sometimes in clean condition and below Western prices. Domestic units are 100V and need a transformer abroad. In Japanese listings search アカイ (Akai) and MPC3000 or MPC-3000, and read the condition terms — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested); on an MPC junk frequently means a dead screen or floppy drive, both fixable. schema.description: The E-mu SP-1200 is a 12-bit sampling drum machine released in 1987, iconic in hip-hop for its gritty sound and short sampling time.

sections.whatItIs: The E-mu SP-1200, released in 1987, is the 12-bit sampling drum machine whose limitations became its legend. Just over ten seconds of total sampling time and a 12-bit converter with analog filtering give it a gritty, punchy character that defined an era of hip-hop, and producers built whole aesthetics around its constraints. It's a sampler and sequencer with sliders and pads rather than a keyboard instrument — a purpose-built groovebox that people still chase for one very specific sound.
sections.buyingUsed: Originals are scarce and valuable, so authenticity and condition are paramount. The sliders and pads wear with heavy use and can need cleaning or replacement; the floppy drive is a frequent failure point (emulator replacements exist); and the backup battery dies like any machine of its age. Test the sliders, every pad, the disk drive, and the outputs. Be aware of the landscape: Rossum Electro-Music (founded by E-mu's Dave Rossum) released an authorized SP-1200 reissue, and various software and hardware emulations exist — none of which are a vintage original, though titles may not say so. Given the values, insist on clear photos and a real account of condition.
sections.regionalNotes: The SP-1200 is American-built, so it appears in Japan less often than home-grown Akai or Roland gear — but it does surface on Yahoo Auctions and through specialist Japanese dealers, and interest there is strong. Voltage cuts both ways: US units are 117V, Japanese-market units 100V, so confirm which you're getting. In Japanese listings look for E-mu or イーミュー and SP-1200; the condition vocabulary is the same — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested). For a rare, pricey machine like this, Brrtz's single scan across Japanese and Western sources helps you see the whole market rather than one corner of it.

schema.description: The Roland SP-404 is a portable sampler first released in 2005, widely used in lo-fi and hip-hop production for its effects and workflow.

sections.whatItIs: The Roland SP-404, first released in 2005, is the battery-capable portable sampler that became a lo-fi and hip-hop staple. Sample onto its pads, mangle with its onboard effects — the vinyl sim, the resonant filters, the cassette-style warmth — and perform or resample on the fly; that immediacy and its gritty character built a devoted following. The line has grown through the SP-404SX, the SP-404A, and the current SP-404MKII, which added a deeper effects engine and modern connectivity while keeping the core workflow.
sections.buyingUsed: This is a modern, robust sampler, so buying used is lower-risk than a vintage instrument, but which version you're getting matters most. The original SP-404, the SP-404SX, the SP-404A, and the SP-404MKII differ meaningfully in features, effects, and value, and prices vary accordingly — read the exact model in the title, not just SP-404. On any unit, check the pads for even response and wear, the encoders and buttons, the screen, and whether it ships with the original power supply (the older units use a specific adapter). For the older SX and A, confirm the SD card slot reads reliably; for the MKII, confirm the firmware is current.
sections.regionalNotes: As a current Roland product the SP-404 line is everywhere in Japan and often the best-value place to buy — Yahoo Auctions, Mercari, and Hard Off list every generation, frequently cheaper than Western retail even accounting for shipping. Domestic units are 100V, though the external adapters are usually easy to substitute. In Japanese listings search ローランド (Roland) and SP-404, SP-404SX, or SP-404MK2, and read condition terms — 動作確認済み (tested working), 整備済み (serviced), 美品 (excellent), against ジャンク (junk) and 未確認 (untested). Because the generations are named inconsistently across listings, Brrtz's cross-market scan helps you pin the exact model and the best price in one pass.
